turns.text: Jalen Brooks, May 21,

turns.text: What's been going on?

turns.text: He caught a cold about three days ago, runny nose, and then yesterday the wheezing started and the cough got real bad. He woke up twice last night coughing.

turns.text: How often has he needed his albuterol?

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Every four hours since last night, two puffs each time. Well, no, he's been doing four puffs. The school nurse told him four. Last time was around seven this morning. And does it help? For an hour or two, then he's back to wheezing.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, and the daily inhaler, the fluted cassone, is he still taking that?

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Um, honestly, no. He was doing so good over the summer that we kind of stopped it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Maybe since June.

turns.text: That happens a lot, no judgment, any fever. No, I've been checking, no fever. Jalen, does your chest hurt? He's shaking his head, he says it just feels tight. And he vomiting after coughing fits.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: No. Anybody smoke around him, at home or in the car?

turns.text: No, nobody smokes. I've got cupped myself, I'm on oxygen at night, so believe me, there's no smoking in my house.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good, has he needed steroids or been in the hospital for his asthma this year? Not this year.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: He had pneumonia two winters ago, but that cleared up, and he's never been admitted for asthma. Any allergies to medicines?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: None. Okay, so his weight today is 30 kilograms. Temperature 99 .1, heart rate 118, he's breathing 28 times a minute, and his oxygen level is 93 % on room air. Let me listen. I hear wheezing all over both lungs when he breathes out, and there's a little pulling in under his ribs. He's still talking in full sentences, which is reassuring. Ears and throat look okay. Okay.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Is that bad, the 93?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: It's a bit low, so I want to give him a breathing treatment right now, albuterol with iprotropium in the nebulizer, and we'll rate check in about 20 minutes.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Okay, go on baby, hold the mask. Alright, it's been about 20 minutes.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Oxygen is up to 97%, breathing rate 22,

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: heart rate 130,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: which is from the albuterol that's expected. Just a few scattered wheezes now and no more pulling under the ribs. That's a nice response.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: He looks better. His color is better.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Greed, so this is an asthma flare, triggered by the cold and made worse because he's been off his controller.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: First, a steroid by mouth.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: The dose is one milligram per kilogram. He's 30 kilograms, so produce alone 30 milligrams once a day for five days. The liquid is 50 milligrams per five milliliters, so that's 10 milliliters each morning. I'll give the first dose here.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: 10 milliliters, five days.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Right, second albuterol, four puffs with the spacer every four hours while he's awake for the next two days, then just as needed.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Third,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: restart the fluted cassone, the 44 micrograms, two puffs twice a day, and have him rinse his mouth after. That one he needs every day, even when he feels fine.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Okay, I'll put it next to his toothbrush. Great idea!

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm updating his asthma action plan, and I'll print one for the nurse at Garfield Elementary. He can go back to school when he's not needing albuterol more than every four hours.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Okay, can you check his insurance is still the same. The member ID is M as in Mary 6620418. Got it, that matches.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: If he needs albuter all more often than every four hours, can't speak in full sentences, his ribs are pulling in or his lips look blue, go to the emergency room. I want to see him back on Friday to recheck and we'll do his flu shot then.

turns.speaker: caregiver
